segments.title: The day that ends the account
sections: The Day That Ends The Account

cues.text: The first trade wins. The next one comes a little faster, from a little further from your level. Then one loses, and the next is taken to get it back.
By late morning the read you had at 9:30 was right, and the day is gone anyway.
An edge, if you have one, shows up in your record over months of trades. One bad day can take the account before that record exists.

So the five hard rules are not there to make you money. They are there so you are still trading when your record is big enough to judge. They predict nothing about price. They are simply on, every session.
Here are the five. One: the trading window, the hours you may trade.
Two: the news windows, the minutes around big scheduled releases.
Three: four reasons to flatten by hand, which means to close a position yourself.
Four: the kill switch, your daily loss limit.
Five: the post-loss reset, a routine you run after every losing trade. It is the one only you can enforce.
The first four are enforced by a clock, a calendar or a platform setting. A platform setting has one great quality: it cannot be talked into anything.
Now, rule one: the trading window.

The window is the hours in which you may place a trade: 6 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern. Inside it sits the focus block, 9:30 to 11 a.m., the first stretch of the cash session, the regular stock-market hours, when your levels meet the most traffic.
Nothing new is entered from 3:55 p.m. The last five minutes are for closing, not opening.
Before 9:30, you may trade only once that day's pre-market sheet is complete. No completed sheet, no trade, at any hour.
The rule: no execution outside 6 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern, and no new entries from 3:55 p.m.
Getting it wrong is one trade at 4:20 because the level was right there. The journal tag for breaking any hard rule is Broke Rule, and winners get it too.
It reveals a trade that came from the screen, not the plan. The fix: the window is the first line of your plan, with an alarm at 3:55.

segments.title: News windows and four exits
sections: Rule 3: Four Reasons To Flatten By Hand

cues.text: Some scheduled releases move index futures in a way no level survives. Rule two sorts them into two tiers.
Tier One is inflation, jobs, the Fed's rate decision and retail sales: CPI, PPI, PCE, NFP, FOMC and Retail Sales.
Call the release time T. Be flat at T minus 5, with no open position and no resting orders, and take no new entries until T plus 2.
Tier Two is home sales, EIA, consumer sentiment, JOLTS and Fed speakers. Manage your position through it, and never exit a working position because of it.
Around a Tier One number price can jump through your stop instead of trading at it. A position held through CPI is a coin toss with a stop attached, and the stop is only a suggestion.
The rule: Tier One, flat at T minus 5, no entries until T plus 2. Tier Two, manage through.
Getting it wrong takes two forms. Holding through Tier One reveals a trade that became a bet on the release. Exiting for Tier Two reveals a trader who wanted a reason to leave.
The fix: write each Tier One time on your plan with its T minus 5 and T plus 2. A position open at T minus 5 is Broke Rule.
Now, rule three. A manual flatten is closing a working position yourself, before its target or its stop has done it. There are four reasons to do that, and only four.
One: the stop was hit. Price traded through it and the order did not fill, so you close the rest by hand.
Two: a Tier One release is within five minutes.
Three: your thesis broke on a candle close. The invalidation you wrote at entry happened, judged on the close of the candle you named.
Four: the session is over. It is 4 p.m. Eastern, and nothing stays open past the window.
The rule: four reasons to flatten by hand. Every other manual exit is logged Too Early.
Getting it wrong is an exit that is none of the four: it stalled, or a red candle looked big. The journal tag is Too Early, and its execution mark, the pass or fail you give every exit, is Fail.
The fix: write one of the four reasons beside every manual exit, and count your Too Early exits each week.

cues.text: This rule is counted in R, so the unit comes first. R is the fixed amount you risk on one trade, chosen before the trade. Every outcome in the journal is in R, so trades of different sizes compare on one scale.
The kill switch is your daily max loss: 2R, twice your base risk. When the day's loss reaches it, trading stops until the next session.
It is fixed: never raised during the session, never adjusted after it fires. It ends the session and nothing more.
Now, where it lives. It only works if your hand cannot undo it at 10:40, so it belongs outside the window you trade from.
NinjaTrader 8 has no daily loss limit. Its Risk window holds templates for simulation accounts only. Live accounts use NinjaTrader's Dashboard.
On NinjaTrader Brokerage, set the Daily Loss Limit in the Dashboard's Risk Settings, and turn on Prevent Changes When Trading is Locked. Then you cannot raise it for the rest of that trading day.
On Tradovate, turn on the Daily Loss toggle, and Lock Risk Settings if Hit.
On Rithmic, the account provider sets the limit, not you, so 2R is a written rule only. Write it anyway: 2R is written, not enforced.
A funded or evaluation account usually carries the firm's own limit. Treat it as a backstop, not your switch.

Two things the limit does not do. It is a trigger that sends a market order, so the fill can land past your number. And it may not see an open loss: some venues count realized loss only, meaning closed trades, so your resting stop bounds the open one.
A loss limit is a smoke alarm. It is loud, and it arrives after the smoke.

When it fires, the account goes liquidation-only: positions closed, working orders cancelled, only orders that reduce a position accepted. Then three steps. Note the time and kill switch in the journal. Close the platform. Step away from the desk.
The rule: daily max loss is 2R, fixed, set at the account level with the lock on, never raised during the session.

Getting it wrong is raising the limit at 10:40, or opening a second account. It reveals a trader trying to win the day back, when the day has become the unit instead of the trade. The fix is the lock, turned on before the session, so a calmer you decides.

cues.text: The first four rules are enforced by a clock, a calendar and a setting. This one is enforced by you, which is why it comes last.

The post-loss reset is a fixed routine, run after every losing trade and before any new entry. It is short, rehearsed, and the same every time, so it runs on a bad day without having to be remembered.

Three parts. First, the cancel. Cancel every working entry order. A resting order placed before the loss belongs to the trader you were before it. If the setup is still there after the reset, you place it again.
Second, the physical step. Feet flat on the floor. One long exhale. Then three or four rounds of box breathing: in for four, hold for four, out for four, hold for four.
Third, three questions, answered aloud.
One: what is the chart telling me?
Two: are any setups forming?
Three: what would need to happen for a setup to present itself?

Answer in sentences. Price is back inside the prior session's range and nothing is at a level is an answer. It's going to come back is a prayer with a ticker. If you cannot answer clearly, the next trade waits.

The pattern this rule exists to stop is the re-entry loop: entries taken one after another without a fresh setup. It usually starts with a win, not a loss, and each trade comes faster and from further from a level.
There is no cap on trade count in this course. The 2R switch is the cap, the reset is the brake before it, and the journal shows your trade count per session, so you can see the loop for yourself.
The rule: after every loss, the full reset before any new entry.
Getting it wrong is an entry within a minute of a stop-out, or an old resting order that fills during the reset. It reveals a trade that came from the last trade, not from the chart.

The fix: before the next entry, write the answer to question three in one line in the journal. A blank line means no trade. And rehearse the reset once on a quiet day, with no position on, so the first time you run it is not the day you need it.

segments.title: One session, three rules firing
sections: Worked Case: One Session, Three Rules Firing

cues.text: This is a composite session, invented prices, built to show how the rules interact. It is hypothetical and not a trade record. Hypothetical results have inherent limits: they are not actual trading and do not reflect real fills, slippage or the pressure of risk.
The pre-market sheet was finished at 7:40. CPI is on it at 8:30, so T minus 5 is 8:25 and T plus 2 is 8:32.
The kill switch is set at 2R, at the account level, with the lock on.
Every trade comes from a branch on the sheet, written before the entry: a level, a read of what price is doing there, a trigger, a stop and an invalidation.

At 7:58 the first trade is open. At 8:25 it is five minutes before CPI, so the trader flattens by hand. The reason is the second of the four: Tier One release within five minutes. Execution mark: pass.
At 8:32 entries are allowed again. Price has moved, and nothing is at a level, so nothing is taken.
At 9:56 a second trade, built to plan, reaches its resting stop. The trader runs the reset: cancels working orders, feet, exhale, four rounds, the three answers aloud, and one line in the journal.
At 10:41 a third trade, again built to plan, reaches its stop. With fees, the day's loss is now past 2R.
The limit fires. The account goes liquidation-only, and the risk settings lock until the reset.
At 10:42 the pull to re-enter is strong. The trader writes kill switch and the time in the journal, closes the platform and leaves the desk.
Notice what the rules did and did not do. Neither loss was a mistake. Both were planned trades with the invalidation written before the entry, and the rules never asked them to win.
They fired at 8:25, at 9:56 and at 10:41. The one decision that was the trader's alone came at 10:42, and the lock had already made it.
The market stayed open after 10:42. It does that. What price did afterwards is not part of the lesson, and it is not your money.

sections: Which Rule Is Yours To Fix

cues.text: Which rule is yours to fix? Score each line 2, 1 or 0. Two means a mechanism enforces it. One means it is written down and you enforce it by hand. Zero means neither.
Line one, the kill switch. Two means it is set at the account level, with the lock on.
Line two, the window. Two means it is on your plan, with an alarm at 3:55.
Line three, the news. Two means every Tier One time is written down with its T minus 5 and T plus 2.
Line four, manual flatten. Two means your last ten manual exits each carry one of the four reasons, or a Too Early tag.
Line five, the reset. Two means it is rehearsed, and the third answer is written before every post-loss entry.

The threshold: any zero is fixed before your next session. The kill switch line must score 2 wherever your venue allows it. A total under 7 out of 10 means the rules are a wish, not a system. Start with the lowest line.
A rule that scores zero is not a rule. It is a nice thought.
Getting it wrong is giving yourself a 2 for good intentions. A 2 means a mechanism enforces it.
Before you trade again, set your daily loss limit at the account level at 2R, with the lock on, or confirm that it already is.
If your venue lets you set no limit, write this line at the top of your next plan: Kill switch, 2R. At 2R, close the platform. That is the whole assignment.

Where it goes next. Every manual exit now gets an execution mark in the journal, pass or fail. Module 18, Journaling and Review, teaches the mark and the weekly count of Too Early exits, and shows trade count per session, where a re-entry loop shows up as a cluster.
Module 3, The Instrument: Futures Mechanics, covers ticks, points and what each is worth: the arithmetic that turns 2R into the figure you type into the setting.
Vendor settings and menus change without notice. If a path in the sources no longer matches your screen, the vendor's current page wins.

check.q: What does a score of 2 mean on a line?
options: It is written down and you enforce it by hand
check.why: 2 is a mechanism. 1 is written and enforced by hand. 0 is neither.

check.q: What total means the rules are a wish, not a system?
check.why: Under 7 out of 10, and any single zero, is fixed before your next session.

check.q: What is the assignment?
options: Set your daily loss limit at 2R at the account level with the lock on, or write the line in your plan
check.why: If your venue offers no lock, write: Kill switch, 2R. At 2R, close the platform.

check.q: Which module teaches the execution mark and the weekly count of Too Early exits?
check.why: Module 18, Journaling and Review.

questions.q: What are the hard rules for?
options: Keeping you trading until your record is big enough to judge
questions.why: They predict nothing about price; they decide how long a bad day can last and what it can cost.

questions.q: Which entry breaks the trading window rule?
questions.why: Nothing new is entered from 3:55 p.m.

questions.q: When must you be flat for a Tier One release?
questions.why: Flat at T minus 5, no new entries until T plus 2.

questions.q: A working trade is nearly at target and a Tier Two print is coming. What do you do?
questions.why: Tier Two: manage through, and never exit a working position because of it.

questions.q: Which manual exit is logged Too Early?
options: A stop hit that did not fill
questions.why: Anything outside the four reasons is Too Early, with an execution mark of Fail.

questions.q: The daily kill switch is set at...
options: Whatever you feel like each morning
questions.why: 2R, fixed, never raised during the session.

questions.q: NT8's Risk window holds a daily loss limit for live accounts.
options: False: it holds simulation templates; live accounts use the broker's Dashboard
False: the limit lives on the chart
questions.why: NT8 has no daily loss limit of its own; the venue sets it.

questions.q: What comes first in the post-loss reset?
questions.why: Cancel, then the physical step, then the three questions aloud.
